To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) drivers' trust and perceived safety of level 2 automation increased after a 30 min drive on a public highway, 2) drivers' engagement was lower for automated versus manual driving, 3) complacency was observed during the drive, and 4) mode confusion occurred when automation disengaged due to interaction with the controls.
driver trust and technology acceptance increase after a drive, while engagement decreases.
the level 2 automation mode in the vehicle we used did not provide sufficient feedback to the driver to inform them of the current mode or the mode changes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of automated driving systems that are both safe and acceptable to users.
the human factors issues associated with level 2 automated driving technology and its use by real world drivers.
how the design of level 2 automation affects driver trust in the system, and the impact that this has on the safe use of the technology.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the study has shown that the technology is not yet ready for public roads.

the driver trust mode confusion in this on road study of partially automated vehicles is due to insufficient cues to inform the drivers of the automation status, which is a result of the design of the system.

the study found that driver trust in level 2 automation was higher following the test drive, however there was a lack of awareness and understanding of automation status, leading to driver mode confusion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

driver trust in level 2 automation technology is not as high as it should be, and that this can lead to dangerous situations if drivers do not fully engage with the driving tasks when automation is disengaged.
the current level 2 technology is not ready for deployment in the public domain.
there is still work to be done in the area of driver trust and engagement with automated driving systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
level 2 automation can be used in unaltered public road conditions, and that drivers can accept and enjoy the experience.
the driver trust mode is not an effective measure of engagement and should be removed from the design of automated vehicles.
level 2 automation can be safe and enjoyable to use, but it can also create risks if the driver is unaware of the automation status or if they become distracted.
